PROPRIETARY-STYLE CORPUS SCAN: I downloaded 719 FY2024-25 BRSR texts (and 798 FY2023-24 BRSRs) from a public GitHub corpus and regex-counted framework mentions.
- IFRS S1/S2: only 2 (0.3%: JSW Energy, Suzlon).
- 'ISSB': 18 (2.5%), of which 15 are a boilerplate SASB footnote.
- CSRD/ESRS: 10 (1.4%), mostly double-materiality references (e.g. Vedanta, Godrej Properties).
- SBTi: 58 (8.1%). GRI: 117 (16.3%). GHG Protocol: 77 (10.7%, up from 6.3%).
- CDP: 29 (4.0%). TCFD: 22 (3.1%). TNFD: 7. CBAM: 5. CCTS: 6.
- 'Transition plan': 9 (1.3%). BRSR Core: 218 (30.3%, up from 18.8%).
Caveats: third-party corpus, not the full listed universe; a mention is not adoption.

Global vendor explainers are EU-centric and partly stale. A scrape of ESG software vendor Sweep's site (~1,424 pages where CSRD/ISSB appear) mentions BRSR on only 2 pages. Its 'FAQs about CSRD compliance' page still states pre-final scope ('1,000 employees and... €50M+ turnover or €25M+ balance sheet'), and 'What is the CSRD' still frames the thresholds as 'proposed'. An India-facing consultancy's ESRS guide (syntropyearth) still says the thresholds are 'under revision'. This is evidence that AI answers built on such pages can give outdated post-Omnibus answers.

key_findings.finding: Indian listed subsidiaries of European groups file BRSRs that rarely reference their parents' CSRD/ESRS regime. In the FY2024-25 corpus, ABB India, SKF India, Schaeffler India, Sanofi India, HeidelbergCement India and Grindwell Norton have no CSRD/ESRS mention; only Vesuvius India cites CSRD/ESRS. Intragroup data requests are not shielded by the value-chain cap, which points to an inbound-CSRD readiness gap.

An EU-level limited-assurance standard for CSRD is due for adoption by 1 Jul 2027. SBTi V2 Category A also requires limited assurance of base-year data. Together with BRSR Core assurance phasing in India, assurance-grade lineage becomes a shared requirement across regimes.

key_findings.finding: ACCESS LIMITS (read first). WebSearch was unavailable: the session-wide 200-call budget was already spent by parallel agents. Firecrawl returned 402 (insufficient credits). The org egress policy blocked WebFetch to rbi.org.in, sebi.gov.in, pib.gov.in, dea.gov.in, ifc.org, carbonaccountingfinancials.com (PCAF), climatebonds.net, ngfs.net, ieefa.org, google.com, bing.com, duckduckgo.com, the major Indian news sites and every competitor site tested (crediblesg.com, climes.io, thesustainabilitycloud.com). The only open route was GitHub: code search plus raw files. So the regulatory facts below come from GitHub-hosted copies of official documents: parsed RBI PDFs, an RSS-fed SEBI circular mirror and a PCAF signatory-list import. News facts come from headlines and summaries in a BFSI news digest repo; the articles themselves were not read. No SERP, autocomplete, People Also Ask or search-volume data could be collected. To restore access, add the hosts above to the environment's Network access allow-list, or choose a broader access level.

RBI issued separate 'Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks' Directions, 2025 for Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks and NBFCs on 28 Nov 2025, as part of its master-direction consolidation. The commercial-bank version is RBI/DOR/2025-26/172 and came into force immediately.
key_findings.recency: 2025-11-28 (title and date from the RBI notification index captured at https://github.com/nikhilenumukkala-boop/circular-tracker, updated 2026-10-01; text from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Brainstormex/RegTech/HEAD/server/src/raw/master-directions/Commercial-Banks-Climate-Finance-and-Management-of-Climate-Change-Risks.md)

key_findings.finding: The Directions are a shell. Their stated objective is to let entities 'carry out comprehensive assessment of climate change risks, integrate climate change risk considerations into their extant risk management frameworks'. But the only operative chapter is the green-deposits framework: Board policy, Financing Framework with external review, use of proceeds, annual third-party verification, annual impact assessment and disclosures. No climate-risk disclosure, scenario-analysis or stress-testing chapter appears in the parsed PDF, which is dated 8 Jan 2026.

Borrower data demand built into the RBI green-deposit rules. Third-party verification must cover 'validation of all the related / required information provided by the borrower'. Banks must publish an annual Impact Assessment Report, prepared 'with the assistance of external firms', using indicators such as GHG emissions avoided (tCO2e), energy savings (MWh), renewable energy generated (MWh), waste diverted (t) and sequestration (tCO2e). A bank that cannot quantify impact must disclose the reasons, difficulties and time-bound plans.

The NBFC version (Id=12940) applies only to deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-D) and deposit-taking Housing Finance Companies. Proceeds must follow 'the official Indian green taxonomy'. Pending its finalisation, an interim list of eligible categories applies, with exclusions such as fossil fuels, nuclear and hydro over 25 MW.

RBI's climate-risk DISCLOSURE framework does not appear to be final as of 1 Oct 2026. The IPSF Annual Report 2025 lists it as a 'draft Disclosure Framework on Climate-Related Financial Risks… Final issuance is expected soon'. Among 372 RBI notifications dated 2026 in a third-party index of RBI notifications, there is no climate-titled Direction or amendment; the three 28 Nov 2025 climate Directions carry no 'updated as on' tag. Caveat: the index covers notifications only, not draft press releases, so a 2026 draft could have been missed. Status could not be confirmed on rbi.org.in.

RBI climate scenario analysis and stress-testing guidance: no final or draft guidance text could be found. The IPSF 2025 report mentions only RBI 'capacity-building workshops for financial institutions on climate stress testing, emissions estimation, and transition planning' and a March 2025 policy seminar. Exam-prep flashcards from March 2026 claim RBI already requires climate scenario analysis in ICAAP. That contradicts the RBI notification index and points to public confusion, which is an AEO opening for a dated, accurate status explainer.

RB-CRIS, RBI's climate data repository, was reported in 'final stages' in Aug 2026. The physical-risk module (floods, cyclones, droughts) is expected 'in coming months'; transition risk follows. RBI has described the transition part as including sectoral pathways and a carbon emission intensity database. This is headline-level evidence; the article itself was blocked.

RBI's Financial Stability Report (Dec 2025) flagged climate risk among concerns (ET summary). In June 2026, Deputy Governor Swaminathan J told banks to manage uncertainty from geopolitics, climate change and AI. Supervisory attention is rising even though rules are not final.

Banks asked RBI for a CRR cut on green deposits to scale green lending (ET, 1 Sep 2026). An SBI report sought priority-sector-lending reforms to boost green finance (Sep 2026). Axis Bank reported ₹45,511 crore of green lending (Aug 2026). Green books are growing, and each green rupee needs borrower-level eligibility and impact evidence under the Directions.

PCAF in India. A PCAF signatory-list import dated 26 Aug 2026 (third-party GitHub copy of carbonaccountingfinancials.com/en/signatories) lists at least 11 Indian institutions:
- SBI (joined Feb 2025)
- HDFC Bank (3 Aug 2026)
- Central Bank of India (5 Aug 2026)
- Bank of Baroda (Sep 2024)
- Union Bank of India (Aug 2024)
- IDFC FIRST Bank (Aug 2024)
- Indian Bank (Jan 2025)
- Indian Overseas Bank (Jan 2025)
- UCO Bank (Feb 2025)
- ESAF SFB (2019)
- PNB (Nov 2024)
Only PNB has status 'Disclosed', and its disclosure document is its BRSR 2024. All others are 'Committed' with no disclosure yet. The import is a subset, so other Indian members may be missing.

IndusInd Bank joined PCAF in Aug 2026, so three large Indian banks joined that month (HDFC, Central Bank of India, IndusInd). Exam material from March 2026 also lists L&T Finance as a PCAF signatory (low confidence). Financed-emissions measurement is spreading fast across Indian lenders, and most have not yet disclosed. PCAF's expectation that signatories disclose within three years of joining is from memory and was not re-verified this session.

India Climate Finance Taxonomy. The DEA released the Draft Framework on 7 May 2025, with comments due by 25 June 2025. Sectoral annexes listing climate-supportive and transition activities are to follow, and DEA said it would then 'release the Framework'.

The taxonomy was still a draft in Jan 2026: IFSCA officers wrote in ICSI's Chartered Secretary that 'India's own Climate Finance Taxonomy remains in draft form', and RBI's Directions say 'pending finalization of the taxonomy'. June 2026 commentary (World Environment Day notes on a Hindu article) still urged government to 'finalise & enact' it. No evidence of a final taxonomy was found up to 1 Oct 2026; this is unverified on dea.gov.in.

SEBI ESG debt. SEBI's 5 June 2025 ESG Debt Securities framework covers social, sustainability and sustainability-linked bonds. On 27 Feb 2026, SEBI harmonised third-party reviewer/certifier norms for green debt with those ESG debt rules, amending Chapter IX of the NCS Master Circular of 15 Oct 2025. The reviewer must be independent, conflict-free in remuneration and expert, and the review scope must appear in the offer document.

SEBI extended the ESG debt framework to municipal debt securities through the Municipal Debt Securities (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (new Reg 4F, July 2026). It also set up a Working Group on 18 Feb 2026 to review the regulatory framework for ESG Rating Providers. ESG-labelled issuance is broadening and ESG-rating rules may tighten.

IFSCA's Framework for Transition Bonds (29 July 2025) targets hard-to-abate issuers at GIFT IFSC. It requires:
- credible entity-level transition plans with measurable GHG targets
- disclosure of the Scope 3 reporting timeline, capex roadmap and locked-in emissions
- mandatory external review
Because India's taxonomy is a draft, issuers may reference EU, Japan, Singapore-Asia, ASEAN or Australian taxonomies, or IEA/METI roadmaps. The ICSI authors explicitly link it to the GHG Emission Intensity Target Rules 2025 and CCTS.

The IMF–World Bank FSAP for India, published by SEBI on 3 Dec 2025, called for granular data and adaptive measures for climate-risk management. That gives an external, authoritative hook for 'data gap' content aimed at bank risk teams.

DFI and foreign PE capital flowing into Indian lenders and climate assets in 2026 brings DFI-style ESG requirements (IFC Performance Standards, ESMS and exclusion lists are standard for these investors; not re-verified this session). Examples:
- IFC $1bn MSME line, $500m already released to SIDBI (Sep 2026)
- IFC weighing $80m in IDFC FIRST Bank (Sep 2026)
- FMO NCDs of ₹380 crore in UGRO Capital and ₹360 crore in MAS Financial (Sep 2026)
- KKR's first climate-transition investment in India (PMI Electro/Allfleet, Mar 2026)
- BII ₹90 crore into UC Impower (Feb 2026)
- NIIF India-Japan Fund planning faster climate bets (Aug 2026)

PE ESG data standard. The ESG Data Convergence Initiative (EDCI) has 375+ GP/LP members (vendor blog, updated May 2025). Its core metrics:
- Scope 1 and 2 emissions (Scope 3 optional)
- % renewable energy
- board and C-suite diversity
- work-related injuries, fatalities and days lost
- net new hires and employee engagement
- a net-zero/decarbonisation-plan metric
These overlap heavily with BRSR Core, which supports a 'collect once' crosswalk.

ESG ratings became a visible funding input for Indian financials in Aug–Sep 2026. Disclosed scores include:
- Kotak Mahindra Bank: CRISIL ESG 72
- HDFC Bank: 77.78 (Niche Ninety Nine)
- Aadhar Housing: 71 (NSE Sustainability)
- MAS Financial: voluntary rating 71
- Can Fin Homes, HUDCO, Yes Bank, SBI Cards and Karur Vysya Bank also disclosed scores
HomeFirst Finance is funding 10,000 ESG-rated homes and plans ₹150 crore of ESG debt to attract sustainable capital.

Financial-sector BRSR filers are publishing FY2025-26 BRSRs with external assurance: Piramal Finance (assured by LKM & Co), IFCI (external assurance), Indostar ('emission cuts'), Aavas, Cholamandalam Financial Holdings and GIC Re. Lenders now have assured own-operations data, so the gap moves to financed (Scope 3 Category 15) data from borrowers.

Sovereign green bonds continue: the H2 FY2026-27 borrowing calendar includes ₹15,000 crore of green bonds (Sep 2026). Offshore climate capital is also reaching Indian infrastructure lenders (India Infrastructure Finance, Oct 2026). Both are headline-level evidence.

IRDAI. No IRDAI climate-risk or ESG regulation for insurers could be found or verified this session; GitHub code search for 'IRDAI climate risk' returned only product and marketing repos. Insurer climate demand is visible mainly through BRSR filings (e.g. GIC Re FY26) and new climate-hedging products (NCDEX launched India's first SEBI-approved weather derivative, RAINMUMBAI, in May 2026). Insurers look like a low-priority segment for ESG Astraa.

Product fit check (local repo singhpratham19/esgtools, read only). There are no lender-facing features: no PCAF/Category 15, lender portal, green-loan impact indicators or EDCI/IFC PS mapping. A grep found one 'financed decarbonization roadmap' subtitle. Relevant assets that do exist: Scope 1-3 accounting, evidence/audit-trail records (67 matches for assurance/evidence/lineage), the supplier module, and TCFD/IFRS S2 and BRSR mappings. Borrower-side content (CFO answering lender and investor requests) fits today; bank-side content needs a 'lender data pack' export.

Content-gap inference (NOT SERP-verified; search tools unavailable). The competitor content documented in the brand context (TSC, Oren, Climes, Credibl, Sprih, Breathe, CBAM specialists) centres on BRSR/CBAM/CCTS software listicles and explainers. None of it was observed addressing the borrower side of finance-sector demand: what PCAF banks will ask borrowers for, the borrower-level impact evidence behind green deposits, or carbon liabilities (CCTS shortfall, CBAM certificates) as credit metrics. This should be confirmed with a SERP check before committing budget.

key_findings.finding: How this research was done: WebSearch had already used its 200-call session budget when this agent started, and Firecrawl returned 402 (out of credits). The egress proxy blocked WebFetch to every regulator and standard-setter tried: sebi.gov.in, pib.gov.in, cea.nic.in, ghgprotocol.org, sciencebasedtargets.org, carbon-transparency.org, eur-lex, gov.uk, epa.gov, zenodo, climatiq.io, ieefa.org, sprih.com and wikipedia. Only github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com could be reached. Evidence therefore comes from: (a) primary standards repositories hosted on GitHub (WBCSD PACT, Eclipse Tractus-X/Catena-X, USEPA); (b) GitHub code search across 23 queries; (c) my own text-mining of a public GitHub corpus of Indian BRSR filings; (d) secondary GitHub documents that cite law firms and regulators. Every regulatory fact below that is not from a primary repo is marked medium or low confidence. All of them should be re-verified on the regulator's site before publication. No search volumes were measured.

SEBI value-chain disclosure (circular of 28 Mar 2025, SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2025/42, as summarised by a 2026 third-party product strategy doc). Value-chain ESG disclosures are VOLUNTARY for the top 250 listed entities from FY2025-26. 'Value chain' means upstream and downstream partners that each account for at least 2% of purchases or sales by value. Disclosure may be limited to the top partners that together cover 75%. SEBI's own pages could not be opened. One detail in the same doc conflicts with my understanding and should NOT be relied on: it says value-chain disclosure becomes 'mandatory for top 1000 by FY2026-27', which looks like a conflation with BRSR Core assurance. My model knowledge (unverified this session) is that value-chain assessment/assurance is voluntary from FY2026-27.
key_findings.recency: 2026 (doc); circular dated 2025-03-28; see also https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/faqfiles/apr-2025/1745399101865.pdf and https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/meetingfiles/dec-2024/1735040682024_1.pdf (not opened this session)

key_findings.finding: My analysis of a public GitHub corpus of FY2024-25 BRSR text extracts. There are 729 files, of which 705 are non-empty and 704 contain 'Business Responsibility'. Only 219 of 705 (31%) report a numeric Scope 3 figure in the Principle 6 leadership indicator. Another 289 (41%) include the question but leave it blank, dash it, or say 'not calculated' / 'in process'. 197 (28%) omit the Scope 3 indicator entirely. Leadership indicators are voluntary. The classifier is a heuristic, checked by hand on random samples. The corpus provenance is undocumented, so treat it as a proxy, not an official SEBI or NSE dataset.

Same corpus, panel of the 612 companies present in both FY2023-24 and FY2024-25 folders: companies reporting a numeric Scope 3 figure rose from 146 (23.9%) to 189 (30.9%) in one year. Scope 3 quantification is growing, but most listed companies still cannot quantify it.

Scope 3 disclosures lean toward the easy categories (keyword-mention proxy). Of the 219 FY2024-25 BRSRs with a numeric Scope 3 figure: 54 mention business travel, 41 employee commuting and 20 upstream transport. Only 44 (20%) mention purchased goods or Category 1. Only 9 (4%) mention supplier-specific or primary data, and 10 mention spend-based methods. The category that matters most for manufacturers (purchased goods from suppliers) is the least evidenced.

Supplier assessment is rare. The BRSR Principle 6 leadership indicator asks for the 'percentage of value chain partners (by value of business done) assessed for environmental impacts'. Across 705 FY2024-25 reports: 121 (17%) give a positive percentage (48 above 75%, 29 at 51-75%, 25 at 26-50%, 19 at 25% or below). 226 report nil, 0% or NA. 158 give narrative only, such as 'developing the process' (Union Bank) or 'not yet conducted formal assessments' (Control Print). 200 omit the question.

MSMEs are a material share of listed-company inputs. The BRSR Principle 8 indicator 'Input material directly sourced from MSMEs/small producers' parsed for 611 of 705 FY2024-25 reports. Median 14%, interquartile range 5% to 29.7%. 186 companies source at least 25% from MSMEs and 76 source at least 50%. Spot checks: Suprajit Engineering 70%, Roto Pumps 47.25%, Shalimar Paints 31%. Any primary-data Scope 3 programme therefore depends on MSMEs.

Emission-factor provenance named in FY2024-25 BRSRs (705 files, mention counts). CEA or Central Electricity Authority: 102. DEFRA or DESNZ (UK factors): 39. Spend-based: 15. US EPA or USEEIO: 8. India GHG Program: 6. EXIOBASE: 1. Climatiq: 0. UK DEFRA factors are cited by more than a third as many companies as CEA, which points to reliance on non-Indian factors for non-electricity Scope 3.

PCF data exchange is invisible in Indian listed disclosures. Of 705 FY2024-25 BRSRs: 0 mention Catena-X or WBCSD PACT, 12 mention product carbon footprint or PCF, 6 mention ISO 14067, 6 mention Together for Sustainability, 6 Higg, 43 EcoVadis, 57 SBTi, 50 'supplier engagement', 5 CBAM and 7 CCTS. EcoVadis is the most visible buyer-driven supplier-ESG signal.

BRSR already contains a value-chain carbon-market question: 'How many Green Credits have been generated or procured… by the top ten (in terms of value of purchases and sales, respectively) value chain partners'. It appears in 263 of 705 FY2024-25 reports. Sample answer (AIA Engineering): 0.

CEA grid-factor version drift in Indian carbon tools. Several independent 2026 open-source tools cite 'CEA CO2 Baseline Database v21.0, FY2024-25 all-India weighted average 0.710 tCO2/MWh'. Others still hard-code v18, v20.0, or 0.82 labelled 'CEA 2023-24'. A third-party doc notes that CEA refreshes the baseline roughly every December. cea.nic.in was blocked, so v21.0 = 0.710 is corroborated only by these secondary sources.

Indian freight and transport factors are old. The India GHG Program's 'India Specific Road Transport Emission Factors' date from 2015 (WRI) and are still embedded in 2026 tools, often mixed with UK DESNZ 2023 factors in the same calculator. This is the Scope 3 Category 4/9 (transport) factor gap for India.

USEPA supply-chain factors are US-specific. They are USEEIO-based, and the latest release is v1.3, published as 'Supply Chain GHG Emission Factors v1.3 by NAICS-6' (a US industry classification). EPA states the site 'is NOT intended to provide guidance on GHG reporting'. Applying these USD/NAICS factors to Indian INR spend without currency, price-year and economic-structure adjustment is a misuse risk. That last point is my inference.

GHG Protocol Scope 3 revision. A Phase 1 Progress Update was published on 31 Mar 2026. It proposes splitting Scope 3 totals into tiers (specific/primary, secondary, spend-based) and a 95% minimum coverage floor with justified exclusions. A public consultation draft is expected before the final standard, targeted for late 2027. A Corporate Standard Phase 1 update was published in Dec 2025, and a possible 16th category ('other value chain activities') is under discussion. These details come from secondary sources; ghgprotocol.org was blocked.

SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2 status is unclear. A May 2026 fact-currency tracker said the second consultation closed on 12 Dec 2025, the final was not yet published, and V2 becomes mandatory for new targets from 1 Jan 2028. A later digest describes V2.0 as adopted by the Board, with the validation portal opening in Q1 2027 and V2.0 mandatory for all submissions after 31 Jan 2028. On Scope 3, a vendor blog (Sweep) describes three target approaches: overarching reduction, supplier/customer alignment, and category- or activity-specific targets. Only 'Category A' companies (large companies everywhere, plus medium companies in high-income countries) must set near-term Scope 3 targets. The sciencebasedtargets.org pages were not reachable.

SBTi Corporate Near-Term Criteria v5.3.1 took effect on 14 Apr 2026, per a copy of the criteria table. It was a non-substantive update to the absolute contraction method for recent base years. V1.3.1 / v5.3.1 remains the live rulebook for 2026 submissions.

EU Omnibus I is Directive (EU) 2026/470. It was adopted on 24 Feb 2026, published in the OJ on 26 Feb 2026 and entered into force on 18 Mar 2026. CSRD now applies only to companies with more than 1,000 employees AND more than EUR 450m turnover, with Member State transposition due by 19 Mar 2027. CSDDD now applies to more than 5,000 employees AND more than EUR 1.5bn turnover, with transposition by 26 Jul 2028 and application from 26 Jul 2029. A 'value chain cap' uses the VSME standard as the ceiling on what in-scope companies may request from value-chain companies with up to 1,000 employees. Whether the cap protects non-EU (Indian) suppliers was NOT verified.
key_findings.recency: 2026-02 to 2026-03; corroborating sources cited in https://github.com/endoergic/the_carbon_book/blob/main/00_FACT_CURRENCY_SOURCES_2026-05.md (Gibson Dunn, Covington)

key_findings.finding: CBAM default values for the definitive period: the binding values are in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621, as replaced by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1740. Mark-ups over the country default are 10% (2026), 20% (2027) and 30% (2028 onward) for cement, iron/steel, aluminium and hydrogen; fertilisers carry 1%. Examples for India: unwrought aluminium CN 7601 10 00 default 1.870 tCO2e/t (Türkiye 1.700, other countries 2.203); grey cement clinker 1.44 tCO2e/t, or 1.584 with the 2026 mark-up. Missing supplier or installation data therefore costs more every year.

The Commission has PROPOSED extending CBAM to downstream products (Dec 2025); it has not been adopted. If adopted, Indian makers of steel- and aluminium-intensive downstream goods would need precursor emissions data from their Indian mill suppliers, which turns CBAM into a supplier-data problem.

WBCSD PACT. PACT Methodology v3 and Technical Specifications v3.0.0 were both published on 30 Apr 2025. Patches followed: v3.0.1 (12 Jun 2025), v3.0.2 (18 Jul 2025) and v3.0.3 (9 Dec 2025). v2.x deprecation was set for 1 Apr 2026. v3 added biogenic and CCU attributes and 24 new properties, and renamed 'assurance' to 'verification'.

The Catena-X (Eclipse Tractus-X) PCF aspect model v8.0.0 (18 Jul 2025) added verification/certification v2 sections, prospective PCFs and mass balancing, with names 'aligned with PACT and TfS'. v10.0.0 (release label '26.09') changed precedingPfIds to strings to be 'compliant with PACT'. Automotive and chemical PCF exchange is converging on the PACT data model.

ESG Astraa's own research doc names the supplier-data gap. Supplier portals everywhere are 'survey-and-chase'. The real gap is incentives: showing suppliers 'how primary data beats defaults and protects their buyer relationships'. 'Scope 3 spend-based estimation needs breadth' of factors. CCTS and CBAM reconciliation is done in spreadsheets, and 'auditor workspaces don't exist'.

Product fit. The ESG Astraa brief's data capture includes 'upload, email-in, phone camera + OCR, connectors, supplier portal'. Its Scope 3 scope is 'the categories the customer can actually evidence', and it states that one activity record feeds the GHG inventory, BRSR Principle 6, CBAM installation data and CCTS. The esgtools repo's SupplierRecord holds spendUsd (USD, not INR), responseRate and status ('Primary data' | 'Estimated' | 'Escalated'). Its seed data tags supplier rows with methodology 'Supplier factor' and sources such as 'Purchase register' and 'Supplier declaration', with quality flags. The building blocks for data-quality tiers exist; INR spend support is a gap.

Emerging competition on supplier-side BRSR. 'Anvil', an Indian SME operations platform, plans a BRSR Core value-chain pack. Suppliers fill one BRSR Core form per period and share it with multiple listed buyers, with Scope 2 auto-computed using CEA 0.710. Planned pricing is Rs 4,990/month for suppliers and Rs 1,49,990/month plus Rs 1,500 per supplier per period for buyers. The doc describes Updapt's portal as top-down, where 'each supplier sees a different vendor's UI per buyer'. Another repo (filebrsr) is building upstream and downstream value-chain coverage tracking.

CCTS context for supplier programmes: about 490 obligated entities have notified GHG emission intensity targets (282 notified in Oct 2025, 208 on 13 Jan 2026). New 'why now' trigger for steel: a MoEFCC draft notification, G.S.R. 517(E) dated 26 June 2026, proposes a Third Schedule of GHG emission intensity (GEI) targets under CCTS. I counted 255 unique iron and steel obligated-entity IDs (INSOE…) in it, with targets for compliance years 2025-26 and 2026-27 and a 60-day objection period. It builds on G.S.R. 739(E) of 8 Oct 2025 (aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp & paper) and G.S.R. 25(E) of 13 Jan 2026 (secondary aluminium, refinery, petrochemical, textile). The gazette text is mirrored in a public CC BY 4.0 dataset repo, which totals 745 facilities across 9 sectors and 26 states/UTs. I could NOT verify whether the steel targets were finalised by 1 Oct 2026. Steel is also India's largest CBAM-exposed good, so this is where CCTS and CBAM overlap most.

CBAM rules verified from the text of Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 of 8 Oct 2025, read from a GitHub mirror because EUR-Lex was blocked. Key provisions: (1) Article 2a sets a single 50-tonne annual cumulative net-mass threshold per importer, applying from 1 Jan 2026. (2) Certificates for 2026 imports are sold from 2027 (recital 27). (3) Article 24 requires the annual declaration and surrender by 30 September of the following year. (4) The quarterly holding requirement falls from 80% to 50% (recital 28). (5) Article 8(1) and recital 19: verification by accredited verifiers applies only to actual values, and the Commission publishes default values. (6) Recital 21: where default values are used, the carbon-price deduction can only reference yearly default carbon prices. Points 5 and 6 create a 'default vs actual' decision for every Indian exporter.

BRSR Core status, from a secondary source: SEBI circular SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2025/42 (28 March 2025) replaced mandatory reasonable assurance with 'assessment or assurance'. The top 1,000 listed entities need it from FY2026-27. Value-chain ESG disclosure became voluntary for the top 250 from FY2025-26 and covers partners at 2% or more of purchases or sales. The original glide path (ICAI study material) was top 150 in FY23-24, top 250 in FY24-25, top 500 in FY25-26 and top 1,000 in FY26-27, with nine BRSR Core attributes.

Competitors are already building pages for answer engines on BRSR Core. Syntropy Earth's page 'BRSR Core Assessment or Assurance: What SEBI Changed' (2 Sep 2026) uses question-form H2s and FAQPage schema with questions such as 'Who needs BRSR Core assessment or assurance in FY 2026-27?' and 'Is value chain ESG disclosure mandatory under BRSR?'. This is the format ESG Astraa's companion landing pages should match or beat.

Proprietary-data opportunity: a public GitHub repo holds text extracts of BRSR filings by financial year (104 files for 2021-22, 553 for 2022-23, 821 for 2023-24, 729 for 2024-25). I ran a crude, unvalidated keyword count on the FY2024-25 set (729 files). 'CBAM' or 'carbon border adjustment' appears in only 5 files, CCTS in 7, 'BRSR Core' in 214 and 'Scope 3' in 521. For FY2023-24 (821 files) the counts are CBAM 6, CCTS 2, BRSR Core 149, Scope 3 557. If validated, these counts could anchor a citable data study showing that listed India Inc. barely mentions CBAM in BRSR despite heavy export exposure.

The egress proxy blocked every competitor, regulator and Big 4 domain tried (crediblesg.com, thesustainabilitycloud.com, sebi.gov.in, pib.gov.in, kpmg.com, duckduckgo). Evidence below therefore comes from: (a) public GitHub repositories, via GitHub code search and WebFetch of github.com; (b) primary-text mirrors on GitHub (BRSR filings, CCTS gazette notifications, SEBI circular feeds) that sibling researchers cloned into the shared scratchpad; (c) SERP observations already recorded in the brand context. To fix this, raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION, add Firecrawl credits, or widen Network access in the environment settings.

PROPRIETARY-STYLE DATA POINT: CBAM barely appears in BRSRs. A keyword scan of a public corpus of 729 FY2024-25 BRSR text files found 'CBAM' or 'Carbon Border Adjustment' in only 5: DEE Development Engineers, Harsha Engineers, Jai Balaji Industries, Ramkrishna Forgings and Vardhman Textiles. The figure for 821 FY2023-24 files was 6. The corpus is a third-party GitHub dataset, not the full universe, and many large caps (Tata Steel, JSW Steel, UltraTech, Reliance, Hindalco) are missing from it.

PROPRIETARY-STYLE DATA POINT: CCTS also barely appears. 'Carbon Credit Trading Scheme' or 'CCTS' appeared in 7 of 729 FY2024-25 BRSRs: BPCL, Crompton Greaves Consumer, Godawari Power & Ispat, Hindustan Zinc, Ircon, JK Lakshmi Cement and TNPL. The FY2023-24 count was 3 of 821. Of 14 listed cement, aluminium, refinery, paper, textile and steel companies found in the corpus, only 3 mention CCTS; SAIL, Vedanta, NALCO, ACC, Ambuja and JK Cement mention neither CCTS nor CBAM. Caveat: these filings came out before the GEI targets were notified on 8 Oct 2025, so the FY2025-26 cycle is the real test.

Industry bodies own the canonical 'how to compute BRSR Core' content. 238 of 729 FY2024-25 BRSRs (about 33%) cite the 'Industry Standards Note (December 2024) on BRSR Core, jointly issued by ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI'. TCS's BRSR links it to a SEBI circular dated 20 Dec 2024. Vendor content therefore has to build on that note; it cannot replace it.

The assurance and assessment market in the BRSR text leans towards certification bodies over the Big 4. Counting firms named within 200 characters of assurance or assessment wording in FY2024-25 BRSRs: TÜV 34, SGS 19, DNV 16, Bureau Veritas 14, Intertek 10, KPMG 10, Grant Thornton 8, EY 7, PwC 5, Deloitte 4. This is an indicative regex count, not a coded dataset.

Sprih is active as a BRSR independent assessor, not just a SaaS vendor. The India Cements FY2024-25 BRSR states 'Independent assessment has been carried out by Sprih' against the BRSR assessment and assurance questions. That puts it directly against ESG Astraa's advisory-plus-platform hybrid model.

Sprih's own content is ungated HTML, aimed at queries ESG Astraa also targets. Known pages: 'BRSR Core vs BRSR Comprehensive' guide, 'CBAM compliance 2026 definitive phase' blog, and a SEBI value-chain relaxation post. An EU-focused 2026 competitive-intelligence scan lists Sprih among CBAM declaration SaaS vendors, alongside CarbonChain, Zevero, Climease and sentra.world. Funding cited at about $3M (Leo Capital-led round per a March 2024 headline). These URLs were cited by third-party documents and not opened in this run.

Glocert publishes an HTML 'BRSR Core Assurance Readiness Guide'. Assurance-readiness checklists are an occupied content format (Glocert, thefootnotes.in checklist, Syntropy Earth article). Evidence-lineage design is not.

Who wins the core non-brand SERPs, per the brand-context checks run earlier in this session. All formats are ungated HTML listicles, comparisons or guides:
- BRSR software: The Sustainability Cloud ('Top 5 BRSR softwares'), Oren (BRSR buyer's guide), Newtral, Breathe ESG ('Breathe ESG vs Sprih'), Sentra
- CBAM software: TSC ('Best CBAM software in India 2026'), GreenSutra, CbamTrack, Seasaw, o2log, Encarbonsys
- Carbon accounting: Climes ('Carbon accounting software in India (2026): an honest comparison')
- CCTS: Oren, Climate Decode, CarbonNeeti, Green Curve
No gated white paper from an India SaaS vendor was seen ranking for these queries.

'AI does the BRSR for you' is getting crowded. Public startup repos from 2026 show new entrants:
- FileBRSR: AI extraction from annual reports. Prices EY/Deloitte/PwC at ₹10-25L a year and Updapt/ESGRisk.ai at ₹3-8L, and claims '95% cheaper, 99% faster'.
- Praxya: 'CA-verifiable data lineage', chemical process factors, ₹3-8L a year. Lists Breathe ESG at ₹5-15L and Sprih at ₹8-20L.
- Anvil: supplier-side BRSR Core value-chain forms.
All prices are unverified, self-reported claims. ESG Astraa's differentiation therefore has to rest on governance and lineage, not on 'AI' alone.

A competitor doc names Updapt the 'closest direct competitor' for the value-chain partner module. Updapt sells top-down to listed companies, which then onboard their suppliers. The stated gap: each supplier sees a different vendor portal for each buyer. The same doc says Convergence (convergence.com/india-brsr-core) ships an assurer 'Assurance Workspace' and PwC iTrust ships a similar workflow, so assurer-in-the-loop tooling already exists.

Small Indian ESG advisories are already optimising for answer engines. Syntropy Earth (a Bengaluru advisory) publishes an llms.txt (updated 11 Sep 2026) and Article JSON-LD keyworded 'BRSR Core assessment or assurance, SEBI circular 28 March 2025, BRSR value chain voluntary, Industry Standards Forum assessment, BRSR Core top 1000 FY 2026-27'. ESG Astraa has no equivalent yet.

CCTS scope is expanding to iron & steel. A MoEFCC DRAFT notification, G.S.R. 517(E) dated 26 June 2026, proposes a Third Schedule of GEI targets for the iron & steel sector (about 255 entities per the CCTS-745 parse), with a 60-day objection window. Added to G.S.R. 739(E) of 8 Oct 2025 (282 entities in aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali and pulp & paper) and G.S.R. 25(E) of 13 Jan 2026 (208 entities in secondary aluminium, refinery, petrochemicals and textiles), the open CCTS-745 dataset counts 745 facilities across 9 sectors. Whether the steel targets have been FINALISED could not be verified.

Phase II textiles is large: about 173 textile units are obligated under CCTS (per the CCTS-745 parse), the biggest block in the 13 Jan 2026 notification. Textiles is not a CBAM sector, yet Vardhman Textiles is one of only 5 FY2024-25 BRSRs that mention CBAM.

ESG Astraa's only indexed blog says '490 entities across nine sectors'. That conflicts with PIB's 'nearly 490 obligated entities across seven energy-intensive sectors'. It is also now stale: the 26 June 2026 draft would take coverage to roughly 745 entities across 9 sectors. The post needs a dated update; that is itself a quick AEO win.

The BRSR Core assurance phase-in is confirmed in ICAI study material (BOS 83914): top 500 listed entities in FY2025-26, top 1,000 in FY2026-27. This matches the SEBI framework of 28 Mar 2025 ('assessment or assurance').

SEBI set up a multi-stakeholder Working Group on 18 Feb 2026 (PR 13/2026) to review the ESG Rating Providers framework. On 27 Feb 2026 it aligned third-party reviewer/certifier norms for green debt securities with the ESG debt securities framework of 5 Jun 2025. Both were read via an LLM-summarised mirror of SEBI feeds, not on sebi.gov.in.

No new BRSR-specific SEBI circular turned up in a mirror of SEBI circulars and regulations covering Jul 2025 to 30 Sep 2026. However, the LODR (Second Amendment) Regulations 2026 of 14 Jul 2026 were not parsed by the mirror, so any BRSR changes in them are UNVERIFIED and need a first-hand check.

GTRI, a think tank, owns the CBAM headline numbers for India, and they are widely syndicated (Business Standard, Times of India, 31 Dec 2025):
- CBAM may force Indian steel and aluminium exporters to cut prices by 15-22%
- steel and aluminium exports to the EU fell 24.4% in FY25
These were cited via third-party docs and not opened here.

Mongabay India (June 2026) reportedly counts 3,000-4,000 direct and 25,000-30,000 indirect Indian iron & steel exporters affected by CBAM, with MRV costs of about ₹25 lakh a year per firm. This sizes the MSME CBAM audience. It was cited via a third-party doc and not opened.

Content-gap signal from an independent 2026 competitive-intelligence scan of CBAM tooling: CBAM is 'a cost-accounting/forecasting problem (certificate liability, provisioning, pass-through pricing) as much as a data problem; crowded on data collection, thin on the finance side.'

Interplay content between CCTS and CBAM (one MRV dataset; CBAM Article 9 deduction for carbon prices paid in the country of origin) shows up mostly in GitHub research repos and exam current-affairs notes, not in vendor white papers. Examples: a 'CCTS & EU CBAM Enterprise Climate Risk Engine' that models CCTS penalties plus CBAM Art. 9, and an Aug 2026 current-affairs note on 'domestic tax rebates against EU CBAM duties'. This is white space for an authoritative, vendor-grade explainer. Legal status of Art. 9 recognition for CCTS: NOT verified.

Big 4 and industry-body content could be catalogued only partially:
- PwC India's net-zero/ESG page has an 'ESG Reporting and BRSR' tab (site mirror), and PwC runs iTrust.
- EY India has an ESG & sustainability assurance services page and has announced use-case expansions of its EY ESG Compass platform (Aug 2024).
- CEEW published an open-access (CC BY-NC) Issue Brief, 'Unlocking India's Voluntary Carbon Market' (Aug 2025).
- TERI publishes open PDFs.
Specific KPMG, EY, Deloitte, PwC and GT Bharat India white-paper titles for 2024-26, and whether they are gated, could NOT be verified in this run.

Trade context, low reliability: a 2026 current-affairs dataset says the India-EU FTA was concluded or signed on 27 Jan 2026. How CBAM is treated under the FTA was NOT verified; check before any white paper cites it.

Saturated topics (many ungated HTML pieces from TSC, Oren, Sprih, Breathe, Climes, Newtral, CbamTrack, Encarbonsys, CarbonNeeti, Glocert):
- What is BRSR / BRSR Core
- BRSR Core vs comprehensive
- 'Best BRSR / CBAM / carbon accounting software' listicles
- CBAM 2026 basics for exporters
- CCTS 'complete guide' explainers
- assurance-readiness checklists
White space (no vendor piece found):
- a CCTS×CBAM single-dataset crosswalk
- data-driven BRSR disclosure benchmarks on carbon-market readiness
- CBAM finance and pricing for CFOs
- an evidence-lineage standard for BRSR Core assurance
- a supplier 'collect once' standard spanning BRSR value chain + CBAM + Scope 3
- governance of human-approved AI in ESG reporting
- facility-level CCTS target-gap analytics using the open gazette data
This is a synthesis judgement drawn from the findings above.

key_findings.finding: METHOD NOTE, read first. Normal web research was not possible in this run. WebSearch had already hit the session budget (200 of 200 calls), Firecrawl returned 402 (out of credits), and the egress proxy blocked every vendor domain tried (watershed.com, persefoni.com, sweep.net, greenly.earth, workiva.com, pib.gov.in, bing, duckduckgo and wikipedia). Only github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com were reachable. All evidence therefore comes from GitHub-hosted material: (a) api-evangelist repos that mirror vendor blog RSS feeds (titles, URLs, dates, one-paragraph summaries); (b) Broser-ai/Sweep, a full-text scrape of 894 sweep.net pages; (c) vibewatch/startup, a Watershed due-diligence dossier whose evidence URLs were checked as live on 2026-05-19; (d) Gazette PDF copies in prakulhiremath/ccts-745. I could NOT verify any flagship 2024-26 reports from Sphera, Novisto, Position Green (for example an 'ESG 100' index), Dcycle, Salesforce Net Zero Cloud, SAP Green Ledger or IBM Envizi. No backlink counts or search volumes were measured. Claims of 'earns backlinks or citations' below rest on observed third-party references, not link data. To unblock: add these domains to the environment's network allow-list, or top up Firecrawl credits.

Sweep's flagship asset is the 'State of Sustainability in Businesses 2026' report, produced with Sustainability Magazine from a survey of 'more than 120 enterprises globally'. Headline stats: 91% produce annual carbon accounts; 65% finish reporting within 3 months; 69% struggle to collect supplier emissions data; 59% depend on spreadsheets; 32% are resource-constrained; only 31% use AI or automation; only 40% say they are well prepared; 42% report cost savings from better carbon data. Lesson: a small sample (n~120) is enough to anchor a citable, press-friendly state-of report.

Sweep splits that survey into gated regional editions: Global, EU, UK, US and Nordic 'State of Sustainability in Businesses 2026'. The 894-page scrape contains no India or APAC edition. This is the clearest proven format with an India-shaped hole.

Sweep's earlier press-driving study: an independent Censuswide survey commissioned by Sweep with Capgemini, released 24 Sep 2024. It polled 554 sustainability professionals in the US, UK, France and Germany. Headline: 81% (more than 80%) say they must transform to survive the low-carbon economy; 78% still use spreadsheets; 72% do not track Scope 3; 61% spend 4+ hours a week on data tasks. The release discloses methodology, country split and revenue bands. This is the template for a headline-stat survey that gets press coverage.

Sweep's evergreen lead-gen formats:
- Interactive tools: US and UK Sustainability Laws Compass ('3 minutes'), SB 253 Navigator, CSRD Materiality Builder, Interactive Guide CDP 2026.
- Sector 'state of carbon accounting' guides for manufacturing, retail, financial services and energy.
- An ESG software buyer's guide and RFP guides.
- An expert co-authored guide, 'Your guide to US climate reporting, using one dataset' (26 Jun 2026), written with former CARB chair Liane Randolph, former EFRAG SRB chair Patrick de Cambourg and David Carlin. Its 'one dataset, four frameworks' framing is ESG Astraa's 'collect once' thesis, applied to the US.

India coverage gap at Sweep, measured by my grep across the 894-page scrape:
- 'BRSR' appears on 2 pages, one of which is a one-line entry ('Mandatory ESG disclosures for the top 1000 listed companies… by 2023') in a 15 Sep 2025 disclosure roundup.
- 'SEBI' and 'CCTS' appear on 0 pages; 'SSBJ' also returns 0.
- 'Singapore exchange'/'SGX' appear on 33 pages and 'AASB S2'/'ASRS' on 10.
The scrape date is not stated, but the content runs to mid-2026.

Watershed's thought-leadership stack:
- 'State of corporate sustainability 2026: AI edition'.
- An AI-emissions guide claiming inference drives more than 90% of lifecycle AI impact and that lower-carbon regions can cut operational AI emissions by 30-80%.
- Monthly policy updates (for example the June 2026 update on Simplified ESRS and Mexico's NIS).
- An RFP guide.
- Analyst badges: 2026 IDC MarketScape leader, Verdantix 2026.
The URLs were checked as live on 2026-05-19 by a third-party dossier; I could not read the reports' contents.

Watershed's total-cost-of-ownership piece 'The hidden cost of manual sustainability platforms' (2 Jul 2026) estimates that typical 2-3 person sustainability teams spend 294-700 hours a year (about 7-18 weeks) on manual tasks such as emission-factor mapping and spreadsheet Scope 3 modelling. It argues total cost of ownership, not subscription price, is the right metric. The format suits CFO buyers.

Watershed's strongest link and citation magnet is an open dataset, not a PDF. Open CEDA (launched May 2025) is a free EEIO model covering 148 countries, 400 sectors and 95% of global GDP. The 2025 version uses base year 2023; it is licensed CC BY-SA, updated annually, and listed in the AWS Open Data Registry with an S3 bucket and explorer. Third-party repos already embed it, for example jianchuanqi/global-lca-asset. Format lesson: a free, licensed, annually refreshed dataset plus a methodology page earns references from developers, academics and AI pipelines.

Persefoni's content engine, from 55 unique blog posts dated 28 Jul 2025 to 31 Aug 2026 in its RSS mirror:
- 'Best X software in 2026' listicles: carbon accounting, Scope 3, CDP, ESG, emissions management, decarbonisation, financed emissions, free carbon calculators.
- Country ISSB explainers: Singapore, Japan SSBJ, Korea KSDS, Australia ASRS, Canada CSDS, Mexico. Plus California SB 253/261, New York, UK SECR and France Bilan Carbone.
- A monthly 'Climate Policy Roundup' (June, July and August 2026) and a Year in Review.
- A free Persefoni Pro tier.
There are zero posts on India, BRSR, SEBI or CCTS. A grep for 'India' across all mirrored posts from Persefoni, Terrascope, Watershed, Emitwise and Normative returned nothing. Caveat: an RSS mirror may not include every post.

AI governance has become a content and trust theme for global players:
- Persefoni: ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI management (24 Aug 2026); 'AI in Carbon Accounting [+ What to Ask Your Vendor]' (21 Nov 2025); Analytics Agent (5 May 2026); Data Agent (20 Aug 2026).
- Watershed: new AI features (24 Jun 2026).
- Sweep: a 'Responsible AI in Sustainability Management' guide.
- Microsoft: a secondary source reports that, per Microsoft Learn (updated 2026-05-11), Copilot in Sustainability Manager was still in preview and 'doesn't support creating any sustainability data'.

Terrascope (Singapore-founded, acquired by XeleratedFifty on 26 Feb 2026) runs an APAC-heavy country series titled '<Country>'s Climate Disclosure Rules: What You Need to Know'. Covered: Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Mexico, Switzerland and the UK (Jun-Sep 2026). India is absent. It also publishes 'The 10 best carbon management platforms for enterprise supply chains (2026)', 'Spreadsheet, consultancy, software or Terrascope?', and timely standard explainers: the GHG Protocol LSR Standard; SBTi Net-Zero V2 (26 Jun 2026); 'Scope 3 reporting may become mandatory' (31 Aug 2026).

Global CBAM content is written from the EU-importer or US side, not for Indian exporters:
- Terrascope's case study: BBR VT, an importer headquartered in Switzerland, obtained primary data from 50% of suppliers and supplier-specific embedded emissions for 80% of imported goods.
- Persefoni: 'EU CBAM: What to Expect' (30 Jan 2026).
- Sweep: 'CBAM: what US businesses need to know'.
Indian exporters are the data suppliers in these workflows, yet no global player in the sample addresses them.

Workiva runs an annual executive survey franchise:
- '2025 Executive Benchmark on Integrated Reporting'. A third-party blog cites it: 85% of executives who intended to disclose emissions will proceed regardless of politics; 97% say strong sustainability reporting gives competitive advantage.
- '2026 Predictions for Finance, Risk, and Sustainability'. A third-party dossier cites it: 9 in 10 finance, risk and sustainability professionals believe leaders underestimate the reporting risk from fragmented data.
This is a CFO-targeted benchmark that third parties cite. Both stats are second-hand; Workiva pages were not reachable.

Microsoft's ungated playbooks travel into AI tooling:
- 'Accelerating Sustainability with AI: A Playbook' (Nov 2023) and 'Accelerating Sustainability with AI: Innovations for a Better Future' (Jan 2025, aka.ms/AcceleratingSustainabilitywithAI2025) are linked from Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework docs.
- A 'sustainable-ai-pdf' folder ships in Azure-Samples/azure-search-sample-data, which Microsoft's RAG and multimodal tutorials use. A third-party demo repo names 'Accelerating Sustainability with AI 2025' as one of its documents.
AEO lesson: open, well-structured PDFs with clear titles get reused by AI pipelines.

Free calculators spread through partner hubs:
- Normative underpins the SME Climate Hub 'Business Carbon Calculator' (per Sweep's 2026 US software listicle).
- Emitwise blogged 'SME Climate Hub Launches Free Carbon Measurement Suite' (3 Apr 2025).
- Greenly runs 'Leaf Media' data stories (for example 'The environmental impact of artificial intelligence'), which third-party repos cite, plus an ebook and webinar library and a CBAM product page.
Calculators and data stories are the formats outsiders reference most in the GitHub-visible corpus.

Glossary and academy pages rank. In the OriginalityAI AI-citation study's July 2025 Google SERP samples:
- Plan A Academy's 'difference between carbon-neutral, net-zero and climate positive' page ranked #1 for one query, though it was not cited in that AI Overview.
- Plan A's climate-risk page and Persefoni's climate-risk explainer also appeared in organic results.
This is weak, anecdotal evidence that evergreen definitional hubs earn visibility.

Analyst reprints are standard authority content. Sweep says it 'led all 17 vendors' in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Carbon Accounting and Management Applications 2026 (blog dated 6 May 2026), while Watershed also claims Leader status in the same report. Verdantix Green Quadrants (ESG reporting 2025; carbon management 2026) are cited the same way by Sweep, Watershed and Sphera. Indian vendors cannot yet use this lever, so it is not a white-paper format for ESG Astraa.

The global field is consolidating:
- Terrascope acquired by XeleratedFifty (26 Feb 2026).
- Emitwise acquired by Green Project Technologies (July 2025, per the api-evangelist profile).
- Diginex signed a non-binding MOU to acquire Plan A (2 Dec 2025, GlobeNewswire item mirrored on GitHub).
None of these signals new India investment.

India why-now, from primary Gazette copies (read first-hand from PDFs mirrored on GitHub):
- G.S.R. 739(E), 8 Oct 2025: GHG Emission Intensity Target Rules for aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali and pulp & paper (282 facility IDs).
- G.S.R. 25(E), 13 Jan 2026: Amendment Rules adding secondary aluminium, petroleum refinery, petrochemicals and textiles (208 IDs).
- G.S.R. 517(E), 26 Jun 2026: a DRAFT notification by MoEFCC under the Environment (Protection) Act proposing GEI targets for iron & steel (255 IDs, including SAIL plants and AM/NS India), with a 60-day comment window.
Total: 745 facilities. Iron & steel is also a CBAM sector, so CCTS and CBAM now overlap on the same Indian plants. Whether the steel targets have been finalised was NOT verified as of 2026-10-01. An independent open dataset of these facilities already exists (CCTS-745, Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21671592, CC BY 4.0).

Pilot of a proprietary-data hook, from my keyword count on a third-party corpus of BRSR text files:
- FY2024-25: 729 filings. 'reasonable assurance' appears in 198; 'Scope 3' in 521 (this partly reflects template wording); 'CBAM'/'carbon border' in only 6 (DEE Development, Harsha Engineers, Jai Balaji, Ramkrishna Forgings, Vardhman Special Steels, Vardhman Textiles); 'CCTS'/'carbon credit trading' in 8.
- FY2023-24: 821 filings, with 161, 557, 7 and 3 respectively.
Caveats: the corpus is incomplete (Tata Steel, JSW Steel, Hindalco and UltraTech are absent), text extraction is unvalidated, and keyword presence is not disclosure quality. Even so, it shows that a BRSR disclosure index built from public filings is feasible.

key_findings.finding: METHOD LIMIT (read first). I could not reach the primary VoC channels the task names. WebSearch returned 'used its web search budget (200 of 200)'. Firecrawl search returned HTTP 402 (out of credits; the user needs to add credits). The egress proxy blocked WebFetch to reddit.com, quora.com, linkedin.com, caclubindia.com, icsi.edu, icai.org, sebi.gov.in, youtube.com, climes.io, duckduckgo.com, bing.com and suggestqueries.google.com. The GitHub search API through gh is also restricted. To unblock, change Network access in the cloud environment settings (environment menu in the session title bar, then Edit) or add those hosts. The usable channel was GitHub: GitHub code search, raw.githubusercontent.com and git clone. So the questions and pain points below come from proxies, not Reddit, Quora or LinkedIn threads: (a) regulator FAQs mirrored on GitHub, (b) Indian ESG and CBAM vendor FAQ and pain copy in public repos, (c) companies' own wording in about 1,550 BRSR filings (a GitHub text corpus), and (d) Economic Times headlines and summaries saved in a GitHub news archive. No Reddit, Quora, LinkedIn, CA Club India or People Also Ask boxes were read directly. No search volumes were measured.

Near-verbatim exporter pain (supplier data chain). EEPC, the engineering exports body, asked the government to mandate accredited carbon-emission data from raw-material suppliers. ET's summary: raw material suppliers 'need to be able to provide accredited carbon emission data but they're unable to provide that due to which exporters can't have test certificates'. EEPC's Pankaj [surname truncated in the source] is quoted: 'We need accredited carbon emission data from them otherwise we can't have test certificates'. ET also says about 70% of India's engineering exports to the EU come from MSMEs. I read the ET headline and summary through the GitHub news archive (abhishekfolder-spec/my-news, 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-08 pages), not the ET page itself.

The government's own CBAM awareness agenda shows the question clusters exporters need answered. ET summary: sessions covered 'applicability and covered products, obligations for exporters, calculation of embedded emissions, data collection and reporting requirements, and accreditation and verification mechanisms', with iron and steel case studies. Read via the GitHub news archive (2026-08-19 page).

Verification capacity and a common misconception. ET (16 Sep 2026) reports that India set up a committee to help exporters meet EU CBAM requirements and that 'this month, Indian verifiers are granted access to the EU's carbon tax registry'. It also says 'from September 2027, domestic exporters will be mandated to submit returns'. That last framing conflicts with the CBAM design, where the EU authorised declarant files and surrenders by 30 Sep 2027 and the non-EU operator supplies installation data. This is a confusion an AEO answer can correct. Read via the GitHub news archive (2026-09-16 page).

Carbon-price recognition is the newest buyer question. ET reported on 9-10 Sep 2026 that the UK will recognise India's CCTS, so British importers can seek carbon-price relief under the UK CBAM. On 1 Aug 2026 ET reported that the India-EU FTA includes a 'dedicated framework' or annexure on CBAM, under which 'India and the EU will engage on taking into account carbon prices paid within India', with support aimed at SMEs. Both read via the GitHub news archive. I did not verify the legal texts of the UK recognition or the FTA annex.

Geopolitical uncertainty is now part of the buyer conversation. India and 17 other members reserved third-party rights in Russia's WTO dispute against EU CBAM, and ET says the WTO Dispute Settlement Body agreed to establish a panel (ET, 28-29 Sep 2026). BRICS leaders opposed 'punitive, discriminatory' carbon border taxes (ET, 13 Sep 2026). Both read via the GitHub news archive. Exporters will reasonably ask 'will CBAM be struck down or delayed?', and the honest answer is that compliance obligations run regardless.

The European Commission's CBAM Q&A is a regulator-compiled list of real stakeholder questions. The mirrored version is dated 24 Oct 2024 (transitional period). Exporter-voiced questions in it include 'I am an installation operator outside the EU. How can I best share data with EU reporting declarants?', 'My supplier is not sending me the necessary information before the report is due. What should I do?', 'Which emission factors for electricity should be used to determine indirect emissions?', 'Can market-based certificates (Guarantee of Origin, Renewable Energy Certificates, etc.) be used to justify the use of actual emission factors?', 'How will the carbon price paid in a third country be discounted from the CBAM?' and 'What are the default values? How does this work?'. I read it via the GitHub mirror NirDiamant/GenAI_Agents. The current definitive-period Q&A on taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu could not be opened (host blocked).

Vendor FAQ on the importer side shows the same supplier-data anxiety. Kinzoku (NL) asks 'What if my supplier cannot provide actual emissions data?', 'Do I need to become a CBAM declarant myself?', 'Can I use the same emissions data for multiple shipments?' and 'What happens if I do not surrender certificates on time?'. It lists mill evidence buyers want ('Mill test certificates', 'Heat numbers linked to chemical analysis', 'Continuous casting records'). Its dates are 31 Mar 2026 for the declarant-application grace deadline and 30 Sep 2027 for first surrender of 2026 certificates, with a 2026 CBAM factor of 97.5%. These dates are secondary and not re-verified against the EC.

Indian exporter-side vendor copy names the paperwork pain. ExportOps AI's problem statement: 'EU buyers asking for CBAM and origin proof — nowhere to file it'. Sylithe's FAQ targets 'What is the best MRV platform in India?' and 'Can Sylithe help Indian exporters with CBAM and Scope 3 reporting?'. Both signal that Indian vendors are already chasing these answer-engine queries.

BRSR Core questions after SEBI's 2025 reset, as phrased in a 2 Sep 2026 explainer (Syntropy Earth): 'Is reasonable assurance of BRSR Core still mandatory?', 'Who needs BRSR Core assessment or assurance in FY 2026-27?', 'Is value chain ESG disclosure mandatory under BRSR?', 'How should a company choose between assessment and assurance?' and 'Is assessment a softer check than assurance?'. Facts it reports: circular SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2025/42 (28 Mar 2025) allows assessment or assurance. Value-chain disclosure becomes voluntary from FY2025-26, with partners defined as those at 2% or more of purchases or sales and coverage cappable at 75%. Value-chain assessment or assurance is voluntary from FY2026-27. The glide path is top 150 (FY23-24), 250 (FY24-25), 500 (FY25-26) and 1,000 (FY26-27). It cites a SEBI master circular of 30 Jan 2026. I read this via the publisher's GitHub repo; sebi.gov.in was blocked, so the SEBI texts were not read first-hand.

Verbatim BRSR pain points in companies' own filings (Scope 3 and value chain). From the FY2023-24 and FY2024-25 BRSR text corpus on GitHub: 'The Company is in the process of initiating data collection to calculate Scope 3 emissions.' (Carysil, FY24). 'For this reporting year, MBFSL has not computed the scope 3 emissions.' (Mrs. Bectors, FY24). 'NLCIL is in the process of collating data for accounting scope 3 emissions' (NLC India, FY24). 'No measurement activity of scope 3 emissions was conducted in current and previous financial year' (Chaman Lal Setia Exports, FY25). 'Value chain partners have not been assessed for environmental impacts.' (Balmer Lawrie, Shree Digvijay Cement, Anjani Portland Cement and others). 'Data on Green Credit generation or procurement by our top ten value chain partners is not available.' (Nuvama, FY25). Using a value-chain 'not assessed / not available / in process' phrase pattern, 26 of 729 FY2024-25 filings matched.
key_findings.recency: FY2023-24 and FY2024-25 filings (corpus committed Feb 2026)

key_findings.finding: Indicative assurance-readiness signal (heuristic parse; low confidence, not publishable as-is). For the Scope 1+2 'independent assessment/evaluation/assurance' note in FY2024-25 filings, my parser classified 423 of 729 files: 247 'Yes' and 176 'No' (about 58% yes). The rest were unparseable. Of the 260 filings where the Scope 3 answer could be classified, 108 gave a figure and 70 said NA, not computed or in process. The corpus is a sample whose selection is unknown. A clean XBRL-based rerun would make this a credible proprietary statistic.

Disclosure gap on the regimes ESG Astraa sells into. In the same corpus, only 5 of 729 FY2024-25 BRSR filings mention CBAM (6 of 821 in FY2023-24), and only 6 mention CCTS or the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. Those 6 include BPCL, Godawari Power & Ispat, Hindustan Zinc and JK Lakshmi Cement; SAIL, NALCO and Vedanta filings in the corpus do not mention CBAM. Verbatim examples: Ramkrishna Forgings, 'Undertaken CBAM Reporting for European Customers in the Financial Year 2024-25'. Harsha Engineers, 'If unaddressed CBAM leads to financial penalties'. JK Lakshmi Cement says its Udaipur unit moved from PAT and 'recently got included in 1 Cycle of CCTS with baseline year 2023-24 and target years 2025-26 and 2026-27'. Caveat: text-extraction coverage varies by file.

CCTS scope expansion (primary gazette text mirrored on GitHub). G.S.R. 517(E), dated 26 June 2026, is a DRAFT Third Schedule that proposes GHG emission intensity targets for the Iron and Steel sector, with a 60-day objection period. I counted 255 steel registration IDs (INSOE…), with compliance-year 2026-27 targets; for example, the AM/NS India Hazira baseline is 2.2701 and the target 2.1695 tCO2e per tonne of equivalent product. Added to G.S.R. 739(E) of 8 Oct 2025 (aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp & paper) and G.S.R. 25(E) of 13 Jan 2026 (secondary aluminium, refinery, petrochemical, textile), the CCTS-745 dataset counts 745 facilities across 9 sectors. A secondary knowledge base dated 19 Aug 2026 still describes steel as being in 'draft amendment status'. Whether it has been finalised could NOT be verified.

Unverified CCTS market-infrastructure dates from a secondary knowledge base (CarbonAlpha SIH KB, snapshot 19 Aug 2026): CERC trading regulations for Carbon Credit Certificates (Regulation No. 205, Gazette 27 Apr 2026); BEE approved-methodology list updated 7 Jul 2026 (12 offset methodologies); BEE Detailed Procedure for Compliance Mechanism v1.0 (Jul 2024). Treat these as leads to verify on cercind.gov.in and beeindia.gov.in (both unreachable here). Whether CCC trading has actually started is still unverified.

CCTS questions as Indian vendors phrase them (CarbonCounsel CCTS Tracker FAQ): 'Is my company covered under CCTS?', 'What sectoral target applies?', 'What is my reporting obligation?', 'What happens if there is a shortfall?', 'Can my project generate credits?' and 'Can I buy or sell carbon credit certificates?'. A CCTS persona spec lists 'What is my modelled carbon position?', 'What is my projected gap/surplus under the selected target scenario?', 'What evidence/MRV gaps exist?' and 'Buy vs Build vs Hybrid'.

BRSR cost and Excel pain as framed by a direct competitor (FileBRSR; vendor claims, unverified): 'Consultants send Excel questionnaires, compile over months'; '337 datapoints to fill (279 Essential + 58 Leadership)'; 'Manual compilation takes 4–8 weeks'; 'Consultants charge ₹5–15L per company per year'. On the supplier side: '5–10 different questionnaires from different buyers, all different formats', 'No ESG team' and 'Risk of losing contracts'. Price anchors: Growth ₹49,999/yr; 'Assurance-Ready' from ₹2,00,000/yr. Its FAQ includes 'How is this different from consultants?' and 'How do supplier assessments work?'.

Assurance-readiness pain as stated by an India advisory site (Northrop India, BRSR Core insight): 'Aggregating verifiable ESG data across decentralized business units often reveals critical gaps in internal control systems'; 'Requirement to establish SOX-style controls for environmental and social metrics'; 'Most firms lack the audit-ready documentation required for ISAE 3000 assurance, leading to qualified opinions.'

Emission-factor confusion is a recurring practitioner question. An India Scope 2 guide (3 Jul 2025) carries these FAQs: 'What is the most reliable emission factor to use in India?', 'How do I handle electricity consumption from multiple states?', 'Can I use international emission factors for Indian operations?', 'How do I account for transmission and distribution losses?', 'What should I do if emission factors change between reporting periods?' and 'What documentation is required for BRSR reporting?'. The guide publishes state factors without citing a CEA database version, which is a content-quality gap ESG Astraa can fill.

Cost pressure figure buyers will ask about: GTRI estimates 15-22% CBAM price pressure on Indian steel and aluminium exporters (Business Standard, 31 Dec 2025, as cited in a GitHub-hosted market-research note). The same note claims un-verified plants face default values '30 to 80% above actual'. That claim is unverified and should not be repeated without the EC default-value tables.

Pain-point frequency across the sources gathered (counts of independent sources showing each pain; qualitative proxy, not volume): supplier/precursor data 7 (EEPC/ET, EC Q&A, Kinzoku, FileBRSR, BRSR filings, ExportOps, Syntropy); assurance readiness and evidence 5 (Syntropy, Northrop, FileBRSR, BRSR filings, ET verifiers); CBAM paperwork and verification 5 (ET awareness session, ET verifiers, Kinzoku, ExportOps, EC Q&A); emission factors 3 (threadsafe, EC Q&A electricity factors, BRSR filings 'emission factor' in 108 of 729 FY25 files); CCTS coverage and targets 4 (gazette, CarbonCounsel, JK Lakshmi filing, CarbonAlpha KB); cost 3 (FileBRSR, GTRI, Kinzoku); Excel or manual compilation 2 (FileBRSR, Northrop). Supplier data and assurance evidence are the strongest clusters.

key_findings.finding: RESEARCH LIMITATION (read first): The shared WebSearch budget was already used up when this task started (200 of 200). My 3 WebSearch calls were refused, and Firecrawl search and scrape returned 402 'insufficient credits'. The egress proxy blocked WebFetch for pib.gov.in, egazette.gov.in, beeindia.gov.in, sebi.gov.in, eur-lex.europa.eu, climes.io, thesustainabilitycloud.com, ieefa.org, wikipedia, zenodo and huggingface. Only github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com could be reached, and I ran 2 GitHub repository searches there. So the sector analysis rests on: (a) Gazette CCTS notifications mirrored on GitHub (primary text, which I parsed); (b) a GitHub mirror of about 730 FY2024-25 BRSR filings, which I keyword-scanned; (c) facts verified by the brand-context researcher (PIB, EC, SEBI URLs); (d) GitHub repos that quote Eurostat, CEA and Ministry of Steel data, which I did not re-query. The following could NOT be re-verified this session: NHS supplier roadmap dates, the EU ESPR/textile and Battery Regulation timelines, EUDR application dates, any CBAM downstream-scope extension, CBAM default values for India, IGBC/GRIHA rule changes, and whether the steel draft has been finalised. To fix this, add the hosts above to the environment's network allowlist and add Firecrawl credits.

CCTS Phase I (G.S.R. 739(E), dated 8 Oct 2025; Gazette CG-DL-E-09102025-266804) set GHG emission intensity (GEI) targets for 282 entities: aluminium 13, cement 186 (131 integrated plants plus 55 grinding units), chlor-alkali 30 and pulp & paper 53. The baseline year is 2023-24, and the compliance years are 2025-26 and 2026-27.

CCTS Phase II (G.S.R. 25(E), dated 13 Jan 2026, published 16 Jan 2026; Gazette CG-DL-E-16012026-269375) added 208 entities. These are 3 secondary aluminium, 21 petroleum refineries, 11 petrochemical crackers and 173 textile units. The textile units split into 60 spinning, 46 composite, 34 processing and 33 fibre. Together with Phase I this gives the 490 obligated entities PIB reports.

Iron & steel is in a DRAFT third schedule: G.S.R. 517(E), MoEFCC draft notification dated 26 June 2026 (Gazette CG-DL-E-02072026-274012, digitally signed 2 July 2026). It names 255 iron & steel obligated entities with registration IDs INSOE0001-0256, a 2023-24 baseline GEI, and a target for compliance year 2026-27 only (no 2025-26 target). The objection period is 60 days. I could not verify whether it has been finalised as of 1 Oct 2026. A Sept 2026 third-party research note also still treats it as draft.

My computation from the parsed gazette schedules (indicative; parsing errors possible):
- Iron & steel draft: about 359 MtCO2e of 2023-24 baseline emissions, implying about 20 MtCO2e of reductions by FY2026-27 (average intensity cut about 5.6%).
- Steel would grow CCTS-covered baseline emissions by about 75%, from about 480 Mt to about 839 Mt.
- 201 of the 255 steel entities emit 0.1-1 Mt (median about 0.3 Mt). This is a long tail of mid-size DRI, sponge iron and secondary producers.
- Steel clusters: Chhattisgarh 62, Odisha 61, Karnataka 33, West Bengal 25.

Sector comparison, also my computation from the gazette tables:
- Cement, integrated plants: 131 entities, about 260 Mt baseline, average cut 2.7% by FY2026-27; mostly at least 1 Mt each.
- Aluminium: 16 entities, about 75 Mt, average cut 4.8%. Primary smelter baseline GEI is about 13.9-15.7 tCO2e/t.
- Refineries: 21 entities, about 82 Mt.
- Textiles: 173 entities, about 18 Mt, average cut 6.5% (among the steepest). 127 of 173 units emit under 0.1 Mt. Clusters: Rajasthan 40, Gujarat 35, Tamil Nadu 17, Dadra & Nagar Haveli 17.
- Pulp & paper: 53 entities (20 in Uttar Pradesh).
- Chlor-alkali: 30 entities (12 in Gujarat).
Textiles, pulp & paper and chlor-alkali are mid-market-heavy, with weak in-house MRV capacity (inference).

The GEI Target Rules (G.S.R. 739(E)) attach costs to data gaps:
- Rule 4: if an obligated entity fails to submit documents, its achieved GEI is taken as its baseline GEI. The whole target gap then becomes a shortfall it must cover by buying Carbon Credit Certificates.
- Rule 6: CPCB imposes environmental compensation equal to twice the average CCC trading price on any shortfall, payable within 90 days.
- Credits issued or certificates purchased = (difference between target and achieved GEI) x equivalent product output.
This gives every sector white paper a defensible 'cost of missing data' hook.

Listed obligated names that overlap BRSR filers:
- Textiles schedule: Vardhman, Trident, Welspun, Arvind, KPR, Sangam, RSWM, Nahar, Banswara, Raymond, Indo Count, Himatsingka, Grasim and Reliance units.
- Steel draft: JSW, Tata Steel, SAIL plants (Bhilai, Bokaro, Rourkela), AM/NS Hazira, RINL, Jindal Stainless, Shyam Metalics, Jai Balaji, Electrosteel, Godawari, Sunflag, Welspun, Prakash, Sarda.
So the same companies face both CCTS and BRSR, and many also face CBAM or EU buyer demands.

Keyword scan of a GitHub mirror of FY2024-25 BRSR filings (700 usable reports) and FY2023-24 (779):
- CBAM was mentioned in only 6 (FY24-25) and 7 (FY23-24) filings.
- CCTS or 'Indian carbon market' was mentioned in 7 and 2.
- Only 2 of 27 steel-classified FY24-25 filers mentioned CBAM (Jai Balaji, Vardhman Special Steels). No aluminium-classified filer did.
This is a large disclosure-readiness gap. Caveats: the corpus is a subset, not all 1,000 filers; the scan is keyword-based; FY24-25 reports were mostly published before the Oct 2025 notifications.

Across both BRSR years, CBAM appears more often in downstream engineering and auto-component filings than in steelmakers' filings: Ramkrishna Forgings, Minda Corporation, Wheels India, Harsha Engineers, DEE Development Engineers (piping) and Thejo Engineering. Ramkrishna Forgings' FY2024-25 BRSR says it 'Undertaken CBAM Reporting for European Customers in the Financial Year 2024-25'. CBAM data requests are reaching Tier-1/Tier-2 component exporters.

Textile and apparel buyer pressure shows in BRSRs:
- ZDHC, Higg, OEKO-TEX or GOTS appear in 9 of 25 textile/apparel/leather-classified FY24-25 filings (Trident, Sangam, Vardhman Textiles, Gokaldas, Kitex, Nandan Denim, Lux, Jindal Worldwide, Axita).
- Only Vardhman Textiles mentions CBAM. It names customer sustainability demands and 'Eco-design Directives and CBAM' as risks.
- Gokaldas Exports reports 87% export turnover to US/European brands.
- None of these textile filings mentions CCTS, although many of the same groups are CCTS-obligated.

Tyre makers CEAT, Balkrishna Industries and TVS Srichakra cite EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) compliance for natural rubber in their FY2024-25 BRSRs. EU traceability rules are reaching Indian auto supply chains outside CBAM. I did not verify EUDR application dates this session.

Real estate & construction:
- 'Embodied carbon' appears in about 10 of 700 FY24-25 filings (4 of 779 in FY23-24). Most are developers: Godrej Properties, Max Estates, Marathon Nextgen, Aditya Birla Real Estate, Signatureglobal, J. Kumar Infraprojects.
- IGBC, GRIHA or LEED appear in 11 of 51 real estate/construction-classified filings.
- Godrej Properties says construction has 'a high embodied carbon footprint' and that it has set an SBTi supply-chain Scope 3 target.
Demand is emerging, but measurement practice is still immature.

Company BRSRs show the PAT-to-CCTS transition and the next sectors in the pipeline:
- JK Lakshmi Cement says its Udaipur unit left the PAT cycles and was included in CCTS cycle 1 with a 2023-24 baseline and 2025-26/2026-27 targets.
- Hindustan Zinc says CCTS targets 'are yet to be assigned' and a BEE baseline study is underway.
Non-ferrous metals beyond aluminium are a likely next wave (inference).

EU imports of CBAM-covered goods from India, from Eurostat Comext DS-045409 as compiled in a public repo (I did not re-query):
- Iron & steel: EUR 4,755.9M (2023), 4,610.7M (2024), 3,649.7M (2025, -20.8%).
- Hot-rolled flat (7208): -56% in 2025.
- 2024 downstream lines: seamless tubes 7304 EUR 205.9M, fittings 7307 EUR 184.8M, structures 7308 EUR 133.4M, tubes 7306 EUR 127.6M.
- Aluminium: EUR 1,666.1M (2023), 835.7M (2024), 903.9M (2025).

CBAM's definitive period started 1 Jan 2026. Other key dates and rules:
- 50-tonne annual de minimis threshold.
- CBAM certificate sales start 1 Feb 2027.
- First annual declaration and surrender for 2026 imports is due by 30 Sep 2027.
- Covered goods: iron & steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, electricity.
All of these were verified by the brand-context researcher via EC pages.

The Ministry of Steel Green Steel Initiative reportedly certified 12.4 MMT of green steel (threshold below 2.2 tCO2e per tonne of finished steel) across 90 units as of 31 Mar 2026. I saw this only through a third-party repo citing https://steel.gov.in/green-steel-initiative; I did not read the ministry page.

CEA's CO2 Baseline Database v21.0 (Nov 2025) reportedly gives an FY2024-25 weighted-average grid emission factor of 0.710 tCO2/MWh, with a combined margin of 0.736. I saw this through a third-party repo citing https://cea.nic.in/wp-content/uploads/baseline/2025/12/User_Guide_V_21.0.pdf. It is relevant to Scope 2 for every BRSR and CCTS filer.

BRSR Core assessment or assurance applies to the top 500 listed entities from FY2025-26 and the top 1,000 from FY2026-27, under the SEBI circular of 28 Mar 2025 as cited in brand context. Value-chain disclosures remain voluntary. This creates cross-sector demand in 2026-27 for evidence-grade data, especially in pharma, auto, FMCG and real estate, which lack CCTS obligations.

Competition for SERPs and answers, as observed by the brand-context researcher (not re-checked):
- Generic 'CBAM for Indian exporters' content is crowded: The Sustainability Cloud, Encarbonsys, Seasaw, GreenSutra, CbamTrack, o2log.
- So is generic 'CCTS India' content: CarbonNeeti, Climate Decode, Green Curve, Climes, Oren.
- I could not check whether sector-specific guides exist (steel CCTS draft schedule, textile GEI targets, CBAM for forgings and tubes, embodied carbon with Indian plant data). They are probably thin, given how recent the notifications are (inference).

Practitioner and academic interest in facility-level CCTS data is rising:
- An open CCTS-745 dataset (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21671592, Aug 2026) consolidates all 745 facilities.
- GitHub prototypes include a cement CCTS gap analysis (May 2026), a JSW CCTS optimisation (Mar 2026) and a CCTS+CBAM risk engine (Aug 2026).
The raw facility list is therefore not exclusive. ESG Astraa's hook has to be analysis, segmentation and data-readiness benchmarks, not the list itself.

Sector pain ranking for 2026-27 (my synthesis):
1. Iron & steel: CCTS draft for 255 plants plus CBAM definitive plus green steel. Highest pain and best fit.
2. Downstream steel and aluminium articles (auto and engineering components): CBAM data requests via EU customers.
3. Textiles: 173 CCTS units plus EU brand demands.
4. Aluminium: CCTS plus CBAM, but few large players, so a smaller mid-market buyer pool.
5. Cement: CCTS for 186 units. Large incumbents have in-house teams, so moderate fit.
6. Real estate: embodied carbon, BRSR and green ratings.
7. Pharma: BRSR Core assurance and buyer Scope 3.
8. Power & renewables: Scope 2 and grid factors for everyone else.
9. Chemicals, FMCG, logistics, IT/ITeS: lower regulatory pain in this window.
IT/ITeS leaders already publish mature reports, and no GLEC or ISO 14083 mention appeared in any of 700 BRSRs.
